mechanisms.title: (RE)GRO(W), Optional Continuation and Stopping
mechanisms.text: We focused on Type-I error safety under optional continuation (OC). Can we also get safety under optional stopping (OS), and what is the difference? The GRO-criteria were chosen to optimise expected capital (logarithmic) growth ‘locally’, within a study. How well do GRO-criteria go together with OC over several studies? To make the questions concrete, we consider a specific set-up with data stream Y j , 1 , Y j , 2 , … Y_{j,1},Y_{j,2},\ldots corresponding to the j j -th study to be performed. In the first study we observe batch of outcomes 𝐘 ( 1 ) = ( Y 1 , 1 , … , Y 1 , N ( 1 ) ) \mathbf{Y}_{(1)}=(Y_{1,1},\ldots,Y_{1,N_{(1)}}) ; in the second study (if it is performed at all) 𝐘 ( 2 ) = ( Y 2 , 1 , … , Y 2 , N ( 2 ) ) \mathbf{Y}_{(2)}=(Y_{2,1},\ldots,Y_{2,N_{(2)}}) ; and so on. For further simplicity we will assume that all Y j , i Y_{j,i} are i.i.d. The set-up slightly differs from Example 3 in which the second study’s data was part of the same stream as the first; at the expense of additional notation, everything that follows can be formalized in that setting as well. The conditional e -variables determining our test martingale are now determined by a sequence of stopping times N ( 1 ) , N ( 2 ) , … N_{(1)},N_{(2)},\ldots . The first stopping time N ( 1 ) N_{(1)} is defined as a stopping time on the first sequence Y 1 , 1 , Y 1 , 2 , … Y_{1,1},Y_{1,2},\ldots relative to filtration ( σ ⁡ ( Y 1 n ) ) n (\sigma(Y_{1}^{n}))_{n} and defines a stopped σ \sigma -algebra ℱ ( 1 ) := σ ⁡ ( Y 1 N ( 1 ) ) = σ ⁡ ( 𝐘 ( 1 ) ) \mathcal{F}_{(1)}:=\sigma(Y_{1}^{N_{(1)}})=\sigma(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)}) . N ( 2 ) N_{(2)} is defined on the second sequence Y 2 , 1 , Y 2 , 2 , … Y_{2,1},Y_{2,2},\ldots , but it is also allowed to depend on previous data 𝐘 ( 1 ) \mathbf{Y}_{(1)} , i.e it is a stopping time relative to filtration ( σ ⁡ ( 𝐘 ( 1 ) , Y 2 n ) ) n (\sigma({\bf Y}_{(1)},Y_{2}^{n}))_{n} , and defines a stopped σ \sigma -algebra ℱ ( 2 ) := σ ⁡ ( 𝐘 ( 1 ) , 𝐘 ( 2 ) ) \mathcal{F}_{(2)}:=\sigma(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\mathbf{Y}_{(2)}) . In general, N ( m ) N_{(m)} is defined relative to filtration σ ​ ( 𝐘 ( 1 ) , … , 𝐘 ( m − 1 ) , Y m n ) n \sigma(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{Y}_{(m-1)},Y_{m}^{n})_{n} , and defines a stopped σ \sigma -algebra ℱ ( m ) := σ ⁡ ( 𝐘 ( 1 ) , … , 𝐘 ( m ) ) \mathcal{F}_{(m)}:=\sigma(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{Y}_{(m)}) . We let 𝒩 ( m ) \mathcal{N}_{(m)} be the collection of all stopping times for the m m -th study, i.e. relative to σ ​ ( 𝐘 ( 1 ) , … , 𝐘 ( m − 1 ) , Y m , 1 , … , Y m , n ) n \sigma(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{Y}_{(m-1)},Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,n})_{n} . The sequence of stopped σ \sigma -algebras thus defines a new filtration ( ℱ ( m ) ) m (\mathcal{F}_{(m)})_{m} , which we call the filtration at the study level , since ℱ ( m ) \mathcal{F}_{(m)} denotes all information available after m m studies or trials have been completed — it is the filtration referred to in Proposition 2 (for the t-test we need to extend this set-up a little, see Example 8 ).

mechanisms.title: OC vs. OS
mechanisms.text: In the optional continuation setting, we assume that, after having observed and analyzed m − 1 m-1 studies, we either stop, or continue to the next study. In the latter case we need to specify a stopping time N ( m ) ∈ 𝒩 ( m ) N_{(m)}\in\mathcal{N}_{(m)} and a conditional e-variable E ( m ) ∈ ℰ ( m ) E_{(m)}\in\mathcal{E}_{(m)} where ℰ ( m ) \mathcal{E}_{(m)} is the set of all ℱ ( m − 1 ) \mathcal{F}_{(m-1)} -conditional e-variables. For example, in the setting of Example 1 , with a simple null ℋ 0 = { P 0 } \mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{0}\} and composite alternative ℋ 1 = { P θ : θ ∈ Θ 1 } \mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{1}\} and N ( m ) ∈ 𝒩 ( m ) N_{(m)}\in\mathcal{N}_{(m)} an arbitrary stopping time for the m m -th study, e N ( m ) , W ​ ( Y m , 1 , … , Y m , N ( m ) ) := p W ​ ( Y m , 1 , … , Y m , N ( m ) ) / p 0 ​ ( Y m , 1 , … , Y m , N ( m ) ) e_{N_{(m)},W}(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,N_{(m)}}):=p_{W}(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,N_{(m)}})/p_{0}(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,N_{(m)}}) is an e -variable for every ‘prior’ distribution W W on Θ 1 \Theta_{1} (here we generalize the notation of Example 1 to allow for data-dependent stopping times). In this setting the analyst can freely choose (or somebody else can impose) any N ( m ) N_{(m)} and any W W and use the corresponding e -variable e N ( m ) , W e_{N_{(m)},W} ; all such e -variables are contained in the set ℰ ( m ) \mathcal{E}_{(m)} . As explained in Example 1 , this includes the choice to set W ( m ) := W ( 1 ) W_{(m)}:=W_{(1)} (re-use the original prior) and the choice to set W ( m ) := W ( 1 ) ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐘 ( m − 1 ) ) W_{(m)}:=W_{(1)}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)}) , i.e. use the Bayes posterior based on the previous studies. We can now interpret our various GRO criteria as each providing a prescription to choose specific elements of ℰ N ( m ) \mathcal{E}_{N_{(m)}} , for all stopping times N ( m ) N_{(m)} that are constant given the outcomes of previous studies 𝐘 ( m − 1 ) \mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)} , i.e. that are ℱ ( m − 1 ) \mathcal{F}_{(m-1)} -measurable. To see this, note that each GRO criterion in combination with ℋ 0 \mathcal{H}_{0} and ℋ 1 \mathcal{H}_{1} defines, for each n n , an e -variable S [ n ] S^{[n]} for a single sequence Y 1 , … , Y n Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n} . In all cases, this can be written as S [ n ] = s [ n ] ​ ( Y n ) S^{[n]}=s^{[n]}(Y^{n}) for some function s [ n ] s^{[n]} ; the function s [ n ] s^{[n]} is what is really specified; we call s [ 1 ] , s [ 2 ] , … s^{[1]},s^{[2]},\ldots an e-specification. If N ( m ) := n m N_{(m)}:=n_{m} , we can thus simply set E ( m ) := s [ n m ] ​ ( Y m , 1 , … , Y m , n m ) E_{(m)}:=s^{[n_{m}]}(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,n_{m}}) . We call this the plug-in method for constructing E ( m ) E_{(m)} from specification s [ 1 ] , s [ 2 ] , … s^{[1]},s^{[2]},\ldots (such specification may correspond to one of our GRO criteria, but in general it could be arrived at in different ways as well) . The running product of E ( m ) E_{(m)} thus constructed provides, via Proposition 2 , a test martingale at the study level. In contrast, optional stopping scenarios usually concern only a single data-level process Y 1 , Y 2 , … Y_{1},Y_{2},\ldots , without any super-structure in terms of subsequent studies. The scenario is completely determined by a sequence of conditional e -variables S 1 , S 2 , … S_{1},S_{2},\ldots , i.e., applying Definition 1 at the data level, such that for all n ∈ ℕ n\in\mathbb{N} , for all P ∈ ℋ 0 : 𝐄 P [ S n ∣ ℱ n − 1 ] ≤ 1 a.s. \text{for all $P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}$:}\ \ {\bf E}_{P}[S_{n}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\leq 1\text{\ a.s.} , with ℱ n = σ ⁡ ( Y n ) \mathcal{F}_{n}=\sigma(Y^{n}) . Their running product S [ 1 ] , S [ 2 ] , … S^{[1]},S^{[2]},\ldots (with S [ n ] = ∏ i = 1 n S i S^{[n]}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}S_{i} ) then forms a test martingale. Recall from Corollary 1 in Section 1.3 that for any nonnegative random process E ( 1 ) , E ( 2 ) , … E^{(1)},E^{(2)},\ldots at the study level (adapted to ( ℱ ( m ) ) m (\mathcal{F}_{(m)})_{m} ) we say that the corresponding threshold test is safe under OC (with respect to Type-I error) if the Ville-Robbins inequality ( 7 ) holds. Extending this definition in the natural way, we say, for a data-level process of nonnegative random variables S [ 1 ] , S [ 2 ] , … S^{[1]},S^{[2]},\ldots , i.e. with S [ j ] S^{[j]} adapted to ℱ j \mathcal{F}_{j} , that the corresponding threshold test is safe under OS (with respect to Type-I error) if again the Ville-Robbins inequality holds (with E ( n ) := S [ n ] E^{(n)}:=S^{[n]} ).

mechanisms.title: Sequentially Decomposable e -Specifications
mechanisms.text: In many (not all) cases, the GRO-specification s [ 1 ] , s [ 2 ] , … s^{[1]},s^{[2]},\ldots forms itself a test martingale relative to some filtration ( 𝒢 n ) n (\mathcal{G}_{n})_{n} : there exist a sequence of functions s 1 , s 2 , … s_{1},s_{2},\ldots , with s i s_{i} a function on 𝒴 i \mathcal{Y}^{i} , such that, for all n n , s [ n ] ​ ( Y n ) = ∏ i = 1 n S i s^{[n]}(Y^{n})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}S_{i} with S i := s i ​ ( Y i ) S_{i}:=s_{i}(Y^{i}) and { S i } i \{S_{i}\}_{i} is a conditional e-variable collection relative to filtration ( 𝒢 n ) n (\mathcal{G}_{n})_{n} . We will say that such an e -variable specification is sequentially decomposable , or seqdec for short, relative to filtration ( 𝒢 n ) n (\mathcal{G}_{n})_{n} ; in all our examples except the t-test (Example 8 ) we can take 𝒢 n = σ ⁡ ( Y n ) \mathcal{G}_{n}=\sigma(Y^{n}) . Seqdec specifications have a direct link with the OS setting, resulting in three remarkable properties: first, assuming still that data are i.i.d., any study-level test martingale process we can construct via the plug-in method (see above) based on a seqdec specification also defines a sequence of conditional e -variables and hence a test martingale at the corresponding concatenated data level Y 1 ′ , Y 2 ′ , … Y^{\prime}_{1},Y^{\prime}_{2},\ldots where Y i ′ Y^{\prime}_{i} is arrived at by relabeling Y 1 , 1 , Y 1 , 2 , … , Y 1 , N ( 1 ) , Y 2 , 1 , Y 2 , 2 , … , Y 2 , N ( 2 ) , Y 3 , 1 , … Y_{1,1},Y_{1,2},\ldots,Y_{1,N_{(1)}},Y_{2,1},Y_{2,2},\ldots,Y_{2,N_{(2)}},Y_{3,1},\ldots in order (so that e.g. Y N ( 1 ) + N ( 2 ) ′ = Y 2 , N ( 2 ) Y^{\prime}_{N_{(1)}+N_{(2)}}=Y_{2,N_{(2)}} ). This defines a concatenated data-level filtration ( 𝒢 t ′ ) t (\mathcal{G}^{\prime}_{t})_{t} with 𝒢 t ′ = σ ⁡ ( Y 1 ′ , … , Y t ′ ) \mathcal{G}^{\prime}_{t}=\sigma(Y^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,Y^{\prime}_{t}) . The corresponding sequence of conditional e -variables is then given by S 1 ′ , S 2 ′ , … S^{\prime}_{1},S^{\prime}_{2},\ldots where, for T ( 0 ) := 0 T_{(0)}:=0 , m ∈ ℕ m\in\mathbb{N} , 1 ≤ i < N ( m ) 1\leq i<N_{(m)} , T ( m ) := ∑ j = 1 m N ( j ) T_{(m)}:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}N_{(j)} , we set S T ( m ) + i ′ := s i ​ ( Y m , 1 , … , Y m , i ) S^{\prime}_{T_{(m)}+i}:=s_{i}(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,i}) . This means that besides engaging in optional continuation, we can also safely do optional stopping at this concatenated-data level, since the Ville-Robbins inequality holds at this level by Corollary 1 . Second, we can use seqdec specifications to extend the plug-in method (which required constant stopping times N ( m ) N_{(m)} ) to prescribe conditional E-variables for stopping times N ( m ) N_{(m)} that are not constant given 𝐘 ( m − 1 ) \mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)} : for arbitrary N ( m ) ∈ 𝒩 ( m ) N_{(m)}\in\mathcal{N}_{(m)} , we set E ( m ) := ∏ i = 1 N ( m ) s i ​ ( Y m , 1 , … , Y m , i ) E_{(m)}:=\prod_{i=1}^{N_{(m)}}s_{i}(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,i}) . By construction, this reduces to the plug-in method whenever N ( m ) N_{(m)} is constant given 𝐘 ( m − 1 ) \mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)} , so it is a proper extension, and it follows as a direct corollary of the fact that E ( m ) E_{(m)} can be rewritten as ∏ i = 1 N ( m ) S T ( m − 1 ) + i ′ \prod_{i=1}^{N_{(m)}}S^{\prime}_{T_{(m-1)}+i} , i.e. a product of factors in a test martingale, that any E ( m ) E_{(m)} constructed in this manner for any seqdec specification is a ℱ ( m − 1 ) \mathcal{F}_{(m-1)} -conditional e -variable. Third, seqdec specifications allow for alternative ways to create study-level processes from e -specifications beyond the plug-in method used thus far. For example, we can set E ( m ) := ∏ i = 1 N ( m ) s T ( m − 1 ) + i ​ ( 𝐘 ( m − 1 ) , Y m , 1 , … , Y m , i ) E_{(m)}:=\prod_{i=1}^{N_{(m)}}s_{T_{(m-1)}+i}(\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)},Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,i}) for arbitrary stopping times N ( 1 ) , … , N ( m ) N_{(1)},\ldots,N_{(m)} . Once again, this also defines a martingale at the concatenated data-level — it is simply the martingale that arises if we view the m m studies as one single, long sequence of T ( m ) T_{(m)} data points. We call this the sequential application of the e -variable specification — see Figure 3 . Summarizing, the practical setting we have in mind when we speak about OS and OC respectively is quite different: OC concerns study-level martingales constructed by deciding, on the fly , after the m − 1 m-1 -st study, whether to continue to the m m -th study and if so, what new ℱ ( m − 1 ) \mathcal{F}_{(m-1)} -conditional e -variable to take from the set ℰ ( m ) \mathcal{E}_{(m)} of possible e -variables of use. OS is about data-level martingales with only a stop/continue choice. Nevertheless, the formal definitions of (Type-I error) ‘safety under OS’ and ‘safety under OC’ only differ in that ‘study-level’ is replaced by ‘data-level’. We may say that combining e-variables E ( m ) E_{(m)} by multiplication is always Type-I error safe under OC. If the e-variable prescription used to construct E ( m ) E_{(m)} has the seqdec property, then the stopping times N ( m ) N_{(m)} used in each study do not need to be specified before the study starts and can even be externally imposed, so that we have Type-I error safety not just under OC but also under OS within each individual study. There is one final subtlety to consider: in the OS setting, with a single stream of data Y 1 , Y 2 , … Y_{1},Y_{2},\ldots and conditional e-variables S 1 , S 2 , … S_{1},S_{2},\ldots and test martingale S [ 1 ] , S [ 2 ] , … S^{[1]},S^{[2]},\ldots , the Ville-Robbins inequality ( 7 ) implies that our Type-I error bound α \alpha is guaranteed no matter when we stop — in particular, the actual stopping time does not have to be taken relative to the filtration ( 𝒢 n ) n (\mathcal{G}_{n})_{n} — we may even peek into the future to decide whether to stop now. This suggests that our care in specifying the correct filtrations for the t-test was unnecessary — it seems we can use any stopping rule we like! But this becomes incorrect once we move from OS at the data-level to OC at the study-level: if, in the t-test setting with the plug-in construction of the e -variable E ( m ) E_{(m)} for the m m -th study, we were to set the N ( m ) N_{(m)} so that they are not stopping times relative to ( ℱ ( m − 1 ) ∪ σ ⁡ ( V m , 1 , … , V m , n ) ) n (\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}\cup\sigma(V_{m,1},\ldots,V_{m,n}))_{n} but only relative to the more refined ( ℱ ( m − 1 ) ∪ σ ⁡ ( Y m , 1 , … , Y m , n ) ) n (\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}\cup\sigma(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,n}))_{n} , we could end up creating fake conditional e -variables at the study-level, i.e. so that 𝐄 P 0 ​ [ E ( m ) ∣ ℱ ( m − 1 ) ] > 1 \mathbf{E}_{P_{0}}[E_{(m)}\mid\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}]>1 for all m m ( ( Perez et al., 2022 , Appendix B) constructs such a random variable for the t-test). And then the Ville-Robbins inequality may not hold any more at the study-level, and we loose the Type-I error guarantee under optional continuation.

mechanisms.title: Local vs. Global GRO
mechanisms.text: Now consider two data streams, Y 1 , 1 , … , Y 1 , n 1 Y_{1,1},\ldots,Y_{1,n_{1}} and Y 2 , 1 , … , Y 2 , n 2 Y_{2,1},\ldots,Y_{2,n_{2}} of fixed lengths n 1 n_{1} and n 2 n_{2} . We may alternatively model these two streams as a single stream Y 1 ′ , … , Y n 1 + n 2 ′ Y^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,Y^{\prime}_{n_{1}+n_{2}} of length n 1 + n 2 n_{1}+n_{2} . If we use an e -variable specification with the seqdec property to generate a study-level test martingale in the sequential way (i.e. not the plug-in way) described above, we will get that, E ( 2 ) = E ( 1 ) ⋅ E ( 2 ) E^{(2)}=E_{(1)}\cdot E_{(2)} constructed for the first two data streams (with E ( 1 ) = ∏ i = 1 n 1 s i ​ ( Y i ) E_{(1)}=\prod_{i=1}^{n_{1}}s_{i}(Y^{i}) and E ( 2 ) = ∏ i = 1 n 2 s n 1 + i ​ ( Y ′ n 1 + i ) E_{(2)}=\prod_{i=1}^{n_{2}}s_{n_{1}+i}(Y^{\prime n_{1}+i}) ) coincides with E ( 1 ) ′ = ∏ i = 1 n 1 + n 2 s [ i ] ​ ( Y i ′ ) E^{\prime}_{(1)}=\prod_{i=1}^{n_{1}+n_{2}}s^{[i]}(Y^{\prime}_{i}) constructed for the single alternative stream. We may thus say that the sequential application of seqdec e -specifications is always coherent : applying the specification sequentially-‘locally’ (separately for both studies) or sequentially-globally (for the concatenated data viewed as one study) gives the same result. For example, the Bayesian W W -GRO specification of Section 2.2 , the GROW specification of Proposition 3 and Example 4 and the GROW and REGROW specifications in the t-test example are all seqdec and hence all have this coherence property when applied sequentially. Sometimes the sequential application of an E-prescription is not feasible or desirable; for example, not all details of previous data may be known. We may then prefer the plug-in application of the E-prescription. Unfortunately, the seqdec property is not sufficient to get coherence for the plug-in method: clearly, if we use the same prior W ( 1 ) W_{(1)} as prior in the Bayesian Example 3 for the first and the second study, this leads to different E ( 2 ) E^{(2)} and E ( 1 ) ′ E^{\prime}_{(1)} , the latter being equivalent to using the posterior of the first study as prior in the second. A sufficient condition for a plug-in application to satisfy coherence after all is that it satisfies both the seqdec property, and further that s i s_{i} , with S i = s i ​ ( Y i ) S_{i}=s_{i}(Y^{i}) as in the definition of seqdec, can be rewritten as s i ​ ( Y i ) = s ′ ​ ( Y i ) s_{i}(Y^{i})=s^{\prime}(Y_{i}) for a single function s ′ s^{\prime} , for all i i . Then in fact the plug-in and the sequential application of the e -prescription will coincide, and coherence is guaranteed. This happens in the subset of our examples in which s [ i ] ​ ( Y i ) s^{[i]}(Y^{i}) takes the form q ⁡ ( Y i ) / p ⁡ ( Y i ) q(Y^{i})/p(Y^{i}) for the same p p and q q , for all i i , as happens e.g. in Example 4 .

mechanisms.title: An Open Question concerning GRO
mechanisms.text: In practice we may very well be in a situation in which OS at the data-level is desirable (see the next section for why it would be), so we want to use a seqdec specification, yet the GRO criterion we are interested in does not give one — Example 9 illustrates this for the 2 × 2 2\times 2 case. We may then try the following approach, which for simplicity we only describe for the REGROW criterion: let E n f E^{f}_{n} be the REGROW e -variable ( 19 ) achieving ( 20 ) with f ​ ( θ ) = GRO ​ ( θ ) f(\theta)=\text{GRO}(\theta) for samples of size n n . We try to find a sequence of e -variables E 1 , E 2 , … E_{1},E_{2},\ldots such that E i E_{i} is a σ ⁡ ( Y i − 1 ) \sigma(Y^{i-1}) -conditional e -variable for Y i Y_{i} and the product e -variable E [ n ] := ∏ i = 1 n E i E^{[n]}:=\prod_{i=1}^{n}E_{i} achieves ( 20 ) to within some fixed ϵ \epsilon for all n n larger than some minimal n 0 n_{0} , i.e. By construction, the sequence E [ 1 ] , E [ 2 ] , … E^{[1]},E^{[2]},\ldots is seqdec and allows for optional stopping, and if we can find E 1 , E 2 , … E_{1},E_{2},\ldots such that ϵ \epsilon is small for all n n larger than or equal to the n 0 n_{0} corresponding to the smallest sample we’d ever be interested in analyzing, we can say that the full process (and not just an instance at a fixed n n ) is ‘almost’ REGROW in the desired sense. The example raises an important question: under what conditions (on model, minimal batch sizes and the like) can we create a seqdec specification that behaves optimally for our desired GRO criterion (as in Section 2.2 with W W -GRO, and in Example 4 , with the GROW criterion) or almost optimally (as in the 2 × 2 2\times 2 example above with batch size 2, with the REGROW criterion)?

limitations.text: In our examples, we have used (and will keep using in the next section) the REGROW approach to first eliminate nuisance parameters, if they are present, followed by a GROW approach for the parameters of interest. ( Turner et al., 2021 , ter Schure et al., 2021 ) find that this gives intuitive e -variables that perform well in practical applications, not just directly in the GRO sense but also in terms of secondary measures such as a power analysis (Section 6 ) or as the basis of anytime-valid confidence intervals ( Turner et al., 2021 ) . Still, it may not always be the best way to go. For example, a REGROW approach for the parameter of interest when a minimum effect size is given may sometimes be sensible as well. Let us consider this a bit further for (for simplicity) the case with a minimum effect size δ + \delta^{+} but without nuisance parameters, as in Example 4 . REGROW would amount here to using E W 1 ∗ = p W 1 ​ ( 𝐘 ) / p δ − ​ ( 𝐘 ) E^{*}_{W_{1}}=p_{W_{1}}(\mathbf{Y})/p_{\delta^{-}}(\mathbf{Y}) with some prior W 1 W_{1} spread out on the set Θ 1 = { δ : δ ≥ δ + } \Theta_{1}=\{\delta:\delta\geq\delta^{+}\} . works.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
works.abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting combined with pre-trained large language models has achieved encouraging results on complex reasoning tasks. In this paper, we propose a new decoding strategy, self-consistency , to replace the naive greedy decoding used in chain-of-thought prompting. It first samples a diverse set of reasoning paths instead of only taking the greedy one, and then selects the most consistent answer by marginalizing out the sampled reasoning paths. Self-consistency leverages the intuition that a complex reasoning problem typically admits multiple different ways of thinking leading to its unique correct answer. Our extensive empirical evaluation shows that self-consistency boosts the performance of chain-of-thought prompting with a striking margin on a range of popular arithmetic and commonsense reasoning benchmarks, including GSM8K (+17.9%), SVAMP (+11.0%), AQuA (+12.2%), StrategyQA (+6.4%) and ARC-challenge (+3.9%).

motivation.text: Although language models have demonstrated remarkable success across a range of NLP tasks, their ability to demonstrate reasoning is often seen as a limitation, which cannot be overcome solely by increasing model scale ( Rae et al., 2021 ; BIG-bench collaboration, 2021 , inter alia ) . In an effort to address this shortcoming, Wei et al. (2022) have proposed chain-of-thought prompting , where a language model is prompted to generate a series of short sentences that mimic the reasoning process a person might employ in solving a task. For example, given the question “If there are 3 cars in the parking lot and 2 more cars arrive, how many cars are in the parking lot?” , instead of directly responding with “5” , a language model would be prompted to respond with the entire chain-of-thought: “There are 3 cars in the parking lot already. 2 more arrive. Now there are 3 + 2 = 5 cars. The answer is 5.” . It has been observed that chain-of-thought prompting significantly improves model performance across a variety of multi-step reasoning tasks ( Wei et al., 2022 ) .

figure.caption: The self-consistency method contains three steps: (1) prompt a language model using chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting; (2) replace the “greedy decode” in CoT prompting by sampling from the language model’s decoder to generate a diverse set of reasoning paths; and (3) marginalize out the reasoning paths and aggregate by choosing the most consistent answer in the final answer set.

mechanisms.title: Experiments
mechanisms.text: We conducted a series of experiments to compare the proposed self-consistency method with existing approaches on a range of reasoning benchmarks. We find that self-consistency robustly improves reasoning accuracy for every language model considered, spanning a wide range of model scales. Arithmetic reasoning . For these tasks, we used the Math Word Problem Repository ( Koncel-Kedziorski et al., 2016 ) , including AddSub ( Hosseini et al., 2014 ) , MultiArith ( Roy & Roth, 2015 ) , and ASDiv ( Miao et al., 2020 ) . We also included AQUA-RAT ( Ling et al., 2017 ) , a recently published benchmark of grade-school-math problems ( Cobbe et al., 2021 , GSM8K;) , and a challenge dataset over math word problems ( Patel et al., 2021 , SVAMP;) . Commonsense reasoning . For these tasks, we used CommonsenseQA ( Talmor et al., 2019 ) , StrategyQA ( Geva et al., 2021 ) , and the AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC) ( Clark et al., 2018 ) . Symbolic Reasoning . We evaluate two symbolic reasoning tasks: last letter concatenation (e.g., the input is “Elon Musk” and the output should be “nk”), and Coinflip (e.g., a coin is heads-up, after a few flips is the coin still heads-up?) from Wei et al. (2022) . UL2 ( Tay et al., 2022 ) is an encoder-decoder model trained on a mixture of denoisers with 20-billion parameters. UL2 is completely open-sourced 4 4 4 Model checkpoints at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/ul2 . and has similar or better performance than GPT-3 on zero-shot SuperGLUE, with only 20B parameters and thus is more compute-friendly; GPT-3 ( Brown et al., 2020 ) with 175-billion parameters. We use two public engines code-davinci-001 and code-davinci-002 from the Codex series ( Chen et al., 2021 ) to aid reproducibility; 5 5 5 Public API available at https://openai.com/api/ . LaMDA-137B ( Thoppilan et al., 2022 ) is a dense left-to-right, decoder-only language model with 137-billion parameters, pre-trained on a mixture of web documents, dialog data and Wikipedia; PaLM-540B ( Chowdhery et al., 2022 ) is a dense left-to-right, decoder-only language model with 540-billion parameters, pre-trained on a high quality corpus of 780 billion tokens with filtered webpages, books, Wikipedia, news articles, source code, and social media conversations.

mechanisms.title: Tasks and datasets.
mechanisms.text: We evaluate self-consistency on the following reasoning benchmarks. 3 3 3 By default we use the test split for all datasets if the labels are available for evaluation. For CommonsenseQA we use the dev split; for StrategyQA we use the question-only set from BIG-bench collaboration (2021) : https://github.com/google/BIG-bench/tree/main/bigbench/benchmark_tasks/strategyqa .

mechanisms.title: Language models and prompts.
mechanisms.text: We evaluate self-consistency over four transformer-based language models with varying scales: We perform all experiments in the few-shot setting, without training or fine-tuning the language models. For a fair comparison we use the same prompts as in Wei et al. (2022) : for all arithmetic reasoning tasks we use the same set of 8 manually written exemplars; for each commonsense reasoning task, 4-7 exemplars are randomly chosen from the training set with manually composed chain-of-thought prompts. 6 6 6 Self-consistency is robust to different sets of prompts and we provide a study in Appendix A.1.2 . Full details on the prompts used are given in Appendix A.3 .

mechanisms.title: Sampling scheme.
mechanisms.text: To sample diverse reasoning paths, we followed similar settings to those suggested in Radford et al. (2019) ; Holtzman et al. (2020) for open-text generation. In particular, for UL2-20B and LaMDA-137B we applied temperature sampling with T = 0.5 T=0.5 and truncated at the top- k k ( k = 40 k=40 ) tokens with the highest probability, for PaLM-540B we applied T = 0.7 , k = 40 T=0.7,k=40 , and for GPT-3 we use T = 0.7 T=0.7 without top- k k truncation. We provide an ablation study in Section 3.5 to show that self-consistency is generally robust to sampling strategies and parameters.

mechanisms.title: Arithmetic Reasoning
mechanisms.text: The results are shown in Table 2 . 7 7 7 The standard deviation of self-consistency is ≤ 0.5 \leq 0.5 for all tasks and is thus omitted in the table. Please refer to Figure 2 , Figure 7 and 8 for the standard deviations under varying numbers of sampled paths. Self-consistency improves the arithmetic reasoning performance over all four language models significantly over chain-of-thought prompting. More surprisingly, the gains become more significant when the language model’s scale increases, e.g., we see +3%-6% absolute accuracy improvement over UL2-20B but +9%-23% for LaMDA-137B and GPT-3. For larger models that already achieve high accuracy on most tasks (e.g., GPT-3 and PaLM-540B), self-consistency still contributes significant additional gains with +12%-18% absolute accuracy on tasks like AQuA and GSM8K, and +7%-11% on SVAMP and ASDiv. With self-consistency, we achieve new state-of-the-art results on almost all tasks: despite the fact that self-consistency is unsupervised and task-agnostic, these results compare favorably to existing approaches that require task-specific training, or fine-tuning with thousands of examples (e.g., on GSM8K).

mechanisms.title: Commonsense and Symbolic Reasoning
mechanisms.text: Table 3 shows the results on commonsense and symbolic reasoning tasks. Similarly, self-consistency yields large gains across all four language models, and obtained SoTA results on 5 out of 6 tasks. For symbolic reasoning, we test the out-of-distribution (OOD) setting where the input prompt contains examples of 2-letters or 2-flips but we test examples of 4-letters and 4-flips (this setting is more challenging as PaLM-540B or GPT-3 can already achieve perfect in-distribution accuracy). In this challenging OOD setting, the gain of self-consistency is still quite significant compared to CoT-prompting with sufficient model sizes. To show the effect of the number of sampled reasoning paths, we plot the accuracy (mean and standard deviation over 10 runs) with respect to varying numbers of sampled paths (1, 5, 10, 20, 40) in Figure 2 . The results show that sampling a higher number (e.g., 40) of reasoning paths leads to a consistently better performance, further emphasizing the importance of introducing diversity in the reasoning paths. In Table 4 , we show self-consistency yields a richer set of reasoning paths compared to greedy decoding with a few example questions from two tasks.

mechanisms.locator: §3.3 Self-Consistency Helps When Chain-of-Thought Hurts Performance
mechanisms.title: Self-Consistency Helps When Chain-of-Thought Hurts Performance
mechanisms.text: Ye & Durrett (2022) show that sometimes chain-of-thought prompting could hurt performance compared to standard prompting in few-shot in-context learning. Here we perform a study using self-consistency to see if it can help fill in the gap, over a set of common NLP tasks, including (1) Closed-Book Question Answering: BoolQ ( Clark et al., 2019 ) , HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) , and (2) Natural Language Inference: e-SNLI ( Camburu et al., 2018 ) , ANLI ( Nie et al., 2020 ) and RTE ( Dagan et al., 2005 ; Bar-Haim et al., 2006 ; Giampiccolo et al., 2007 ; Bentivogli et al., 2009 ) . The results over PaLM-540B are shown in Table 5 . For some tasks (e.g., ANLI-R1, e-SNLI, RTE), adding chain-of-thought does hurt performance compared to standard prompting ( Brown et al., 2020 ) , but self-consistency is able to robustly boost the performance and outperform standard prompting, making it a reliable way to add rationales in few-shot in-context learning for common NLP tasks.

mechanisms.title: Compare to other existing approaches / Additional Studies
mechanisms.text: We conduct a set of additional studies and show that self-consistency significantly outperforms existing methods including sample-and-rank, beam search, and ensemble-based approaches. We conducted a number of additional experiments to analyze different aspects of the self-consistency method, including its robustness to sampling strategies and parameters, and how it works with imperfect prompts and non-natural-language reasoning paths.

mechanisms.locator: §Self-Consistency is Robust to Sampling Strategies and Scaling
mechanisms.title: Self-Consistency is Robust to Sampling Strategies and Scaling
mechanisms.text: We show self-consistency is robust to sampling strategies and parameters, by varying T T in temperature sampling ( Ackley et al., 1985 ; Ficler & Goldberg, 2017 ) , k k in top- k k sampling ( Fan et al., 2018 ; Holtzman et al., 2018 ; Radford et al., 2019 ) , and p p in nucleus sampling ( Holtzman et al., 2020 ) , over PaLM-540B in Figure 4 (left). Figure 4 (right) shows that self-consistency robustly improves performance across all scales for the LaMDA-137B model series. The gain is relatively lower for smaller models due to certain abilities (e.g., arithmetic) only emerge when the model reaches a sufficient scale ( Brown et al., 2020 ) .

sections.title: Self-Consistency is Robust to Sampling Strategies and Scaling

mechanisms.title: Self-Consistency Improves Robustness to Imperfect Prompts
mechanisms.text: For few-shot learning with manually constructed prompts, human annotators sometimes make minor mistakes when creating the prompts. We further study if self-consistency can help improve a language model’s robustness to imperfect prompts. 9 9 9 We use the same prompts as before, but swap all the numbers in the reasoning paths with random numbers except the final answer, e.g., from “ There are 3 cars in the parking lot already. 2 more arrive. Now there are 3 + 2 = 5 cars. ” to “ There are 7 cars in the parking lot already. 6 more arrive. Now there are 7 + 6 = 5 cars. ”. We show the results in Table 8 : while imperfect prompts decrease accuracy with greedy decoding (17.1 → \rightarrow 14.9), self-consistency can fill in the gaps and robustly improve the results. Additionally, we found that the consistency (in terms of % of decodes agreeing with the final aggregated answer) is highly correlated with accuracy (Figure 8 , over GSM8K). This suggests that one can use self-consistency to provide an uncertainty estimate of the model in its generated solutions. In other words, one can use low consistency as an indicator that the model has low confidence; i.e., self-consistency confers some ability for the model to “know when it doesn’t know”.

sections.title: Self-Consistency Improves Robustness to Imperfect Prompts

mechanisms.locator: §Self-Consistency Works for Non-Natural-Language Reasoning Paths and Zero-shot CoT
mechanisms.title: Self-Consistency Works for Non-Natural-Language Reasoning Paths and Zero-shot CoT
mechanisms.text: We also tested the generality of the self-consistency concept to alternative forms of intermediate reasoning like equations (e.g., from “ There are 3 cars in the parking lot already. 2 more arrive. Now there are 3 + 2 = 5 cars. ” to “ 3 + 2 = 5 ”). The results are shown in Table 8 (“Prompt with equations”): self-consistency still improves accuracy by generating intermediate equations; however, compared to generating natural language reasoning paths, the gain is smaller since the equations are much shorter and less opportunity remains for generating diversity in the decoding process. In addition, we tested self-consistency with zero-shot chain-of-thought ( Kojima et al., 2022 ) and show that self-consistency works for zero-shot CoT as well and improves the results significantly (+26.2%) in Table 8 .

sections.locator: §Self-Consistency Works for Non-Natural-Language Reasoning Paths and Zero-shot CoT
sections.title: Self-Consistency Works for Non-Natural-Language Reasoning Paths and Zero-shot CoT

limitations.text: We introduced a simple yet effective method called self-consistency, and observed that it significantly improves accuracy in a range of arithmetic and commonsense reasoning tasks, across four large language models with varying scales. Beyond accuracy gains, self-consistency is also useful for collecting rationales when performing reasoning tasks with language models, and for providing uncertainty estimates and improved calibration of language model outputs.

mechanisms.title: Testing using Markov’s inequality
mechanisms.text: As mentioned before, e-values can be interpreted in their own right as evidence against the null hypothesis without resort to other concepts. However, the reader may naturally be curious how exactly e-values may be transformed (perhaps with some loss of efficiency) into the more classical concepts of level- α \alpha tests and p-values. It is in this context that a central role will be played by Markov’s inequality (though it apparently was discovered by Chebyshev, Markov’s advisor). Markov’s inequality guarantees that a test rejecting an e-value larger than 1 / α 1/\alpha yields a level- α \alpha test. The proof follows directly from the simple inequality 𝟙 { x ≥ 1 } ≤ x \mathds{1}_{\{x\geq 1\}}\leq x for all x ≥ 0 x\geq 0 , by observing that For an e-variable E E and a p-variable P P , even though 1 / E 1/E is a p-variable, 1 / P 1/P is generally not an e-variable; in fact 1 / P 1/P has infinite mean if P P is exact. The p-variable 1 / E 1/E is conservative since it cannot be uniformly distributed on [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , and it is typically far away from being so. As a consequence, the type-I error of the test 𝟙 { E ≥ 1 / α } \mathds{1}_{\{E\geq 1/\alpha\}} for ℙ \mathbb{P} is usually smaller than α \alpha unless E E is distributed on the two points 0 0 and 1 / α 1/\alpha with mean 1 1 under ℙ \mathbb{P} . Proposition 2.1 can be generalized in several different directions relevant for testing with e-values; some are presented in Section 2.4 and Chapters 5 and 15 . A sequential generalization, called Ville’s inequality, is presented in Chapter 7 . With a p-variable P P and an e-variable E E for the same hypothesis, the tests 𝟙 { E ≥ 1 / α } \mathds{1}_{\{E\geq 1/\alpha\}} and 𝟙 { P ≤ α } \mathds{1}_{\{P\leq\alpha\}} are in general different, except for the special case E = 𝟙 { P ≤ α } / α E=\mathds{1}_{\{P\leq\alpha\}}/\alpha (see Section 3.1 for more details on such e-variables). To understand how these two tests differ, we consider the two-sided normal test in Section 1.6 , where a family of e-variables E n E_{n} is given by ( 1.3 ), indexed by δ > 0 \delta>0 , and the p-variable P n P_{n} is given by ( 1.4 ). We treat both the e-variables and the p-variable as functions of the value x x taken by the statistic Z Z . Figure 2.2 illustrates two intervals [ A 1 , A 2 ] [A_{1},A_{2}] and [ B 1 , B 2 ] [B_{1},B_{2}] , which correspond to P n ​ ( x ) = 0.01 P_{n}(x)=0.01 for x = A 1 x=A_{1} or x = A 2 x=A_{2} and E n ​ ( x ) = 100 E_{n}(x)=100 for x = B 1 x=B_{1} or x = B 2 x=B_{2} , with δ = 3 \delta=3 . Here, A 2 = | A 1 | ≈ 2.58 A_{2}=|A_{1}|\approx 2.58 and B 2 = | B 1 | ≈ 3.27 B_{2}=|B_{1}|\approx 3.27 . Other choices of δ \delta lead to different intervals, as shown in Figure 2.2 . We can see that it is harder for an e-value to reach 100 100 compared to a p-value to reach 0.01 0.01 , and this is because the Markov inequality is generally conservative. It is generally unfair to directly compare the values of E E and 1 / P 1/P . See Section 2.7 for more discussions on this point.

mechanisms.title: Testing using distributional knowledge
mechanisms.text: Proposition 2.1 implies that for an e-variable E E and α ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \alpha\in(0,1) , we can always reject the null hypothesis by using the level- α \alpha test 𝟙 { E ≥ 1 / α } \mathds{1}_{\{E\geq 1/\alpha\}} . If the distribution of E E under the null hypothesis is known or computable (there may be multiple distributions if the null is composite), then we can find thresholds that are smaller than 1 / α 1/\alpha to test based on E E . Denote by S ⁡ ( ⋅ , ℙ ) S(\cdot;\mathbb{P}) the left-continuous survival function of E E under ℙ ∈ 𝒫 \mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P} , that is, for x ∈ ℝ . x\in\mathbb{R}. If S ⁡ ( ⋅ , ℙ ) S(\cdot;\mathbb{P}) is the same across ℙ ∈ 𝒫 \mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P} , then E E is called pivotal (this will appear again in Section 14.3 ). The function S ⁡ ( ⋅ , ℙ ) S(\cdot;\mathbb{P}) can be continuous or discontinuous, depending on both E E and ℙ \mathbb{P} . For a threshold t > 0 t>0 , we would like the test 𝟙 { E ≥ t } \mathds{1}_{\{E\geq t\}} to have level α \alpha . Clearly, choosing t ≥ 1 / α t\geq 1/\alpha is sufficient, but we can do better. Indeed, by definition, as long as sup ℙ ∈ 𝒫 S ⁡ ( t | ℙ ) ≤ α \sup_{\mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P}}S(t|\mathbb{P})\leq\alpha , t t is a valid threshold for the test 𝟙 { E ≥ t } \mathds{1}_{\{E\geq t\}} with level α \alpha . If sup ℙ ∈ 𝒫 S ⁡ ( t | ℙ ) \sup_{\mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P}}S(t|\mathbb{P}) is continuous, then the smallest t t that satisfies this condition is which is also equal to the largest left α \alpha -quantile of E E over ℙ ∈ 𝒫 \mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P} (Lemma 15.1 in Section 15.1 ). In particular, if 𝒫 = { ℙ } \mathcal{P}=\{\mathbb{P}\} is simple, then we can easily see that which is the left α \alpha -quantile of E E under ℙ \mathbb{P} . The level- α \alpha guarantee of 𝟙 { E ≥ t ∗ } \mathds{1}_{\{E\geq t^{*}\}} requires t ↦ sup ℙ ∈ 𝒫 S ⁡ ( t | ℙ ) t\mapsto\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P}}S(t|\mathbb{P}) to be continuous at t ∗ t^{*} ; otherwise we can use the test 𝟙 { E > t ∗ } \mathds{1}_{\{E>t^{*}\}} , or a suitable randomization between 𝟙 { E > t ∗ } \mathds{1}_{\{E>t^{*}\}} and 𝟙 { E ≥ t ∗ } \mathds{1}_{\{E\geq t^{*}\}} (analogously to the Neyman–Pearson lemma). Reducing the threshold in the above manner is in fact no different from treating the e-value as any other test statistic and picking the threshold appropriately to derive a level- α \alpha test, as is standard in classical statistics. Even in situations where S ⁡ ( ⋅ , ℙ ) S(\cdot;\mathbb{P}) is difficult to fully specify or compute, bounds on t ∗ t^{*} may be obtained based on partial information of the distribution of the e-value. Several concrete cases will be studied in Chapter 15 .

mechanisms.locator: §2.3 Relating p-values and e-values using calibrators
mechanisms.title: Relating p-values and e-values using calibrators
mechanisms.text: P-values and e-values can be converted between each other, via calibrators. Below, when we say “any hypothesis”, we mean any specification of the sample space ( Ω , ℱ ) (\Omega,\mathcal{F}) and hypothesis 𝒫 \mathcal{P} on the space. A p-to-e calibrator is a decreasing function f : [ 0 , ∞ ) → [ 0 , ∞ ] f:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty] satisfying f = 0 f=0 on ( 1 , ∞ ) (1,\infty) such that for any hypothesis, f ⁡ ( P ) f(P) is an e-variable for any p-variable P P . An e-to-p calibrator is a decreasing function g : [ 0 , ∞ ] → [ 0 , ∞ ) g:[0,\infty]\to[0,\infty) such that for any hypothesis, g ⁡ ( E ) g(E) is a p-variable for any e-variable E E . A calibrator f f is said to dominate a calibrator g g if f ≥ g f\geq g (p-to-e) or f ≤ g f\leq g (e-to-p), and the domination is strict if further f ≠ g f\neq g . A calibrator is admissible if it is not strictly dominated by any other calibrator. We often omit “p-to-e” in “p-to-e calibrators” and simply call them calibrators, for a reason that will be made clear soon in Propositions 2.4 and 2.5 . The interval [ 0 , ∞ ) [0,\infty) can be safely replaced by [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] in the above definitions since p-values with values larger than 1 1 are not interesting for testing. A probability measure ℙ \mathbb{P} (or the corresponding probability space) is called atomless if there exists a continuously distributed random variable (e.g., uniform, normal) under ℙ \mathbb{P} . Hence, when we encounter a continuously distributed random variable, implicitly the probability measure is assumed atomless. In Definition 2.3 , the property of calibrators needs to hold for any hypothesis. Nevertheless, it suffices to consider one atomless probability measure ℙ \mathbb{P} on some ( Ω , ℱ ) (\Omega,\mathcal{F}) , because if for the simple hypothesis ℙ \mathbb{P} , f ⁡ ( P ) f(P) is an e-variable for any p-variable P P , then it holds also for any other, simple or composite, hypotheses. This observation will be useful in several places throughout. A formal justification of this simplification is presented in Appendix A.1 . In the next two results we characterize all admissible calibrators in both directions. We first look at the simpler direction. The following proposition says that there is, essentially, only one e-to-p calibrator, f : t ↦ min ⁡ ( 1 , 1 / t ) f:t\mapsto\min(1,1/t) , that is offered by Markov’s inequality. Instead of working with the set of all e-variables, we can also consider conditional e-to-p calibrators that are valid only on some subset ℰ \mathcal{E} of e-variables, which is a weaker requirement, and such calibrators depend on the choice of ℰ \mathcal{E} . This topic is treated in Chapter 15 . In sharp contrast to the uniqueness of the admissible e-to-p calibrator, the class of p-to-e calibrators is much richer. In the context of this proposition, being upper semicontinuous is equivalent to being left-continuous. Below we present some simple examples of admissible p-to-e calibrators. We only specify them on ( 0 , 1 ] (0,1] , as they are ∞ \infty at 0 0 and 0 0 on ( 1 , ∞ ) (1,\infty) . These calibrators include the power form Converting a p-value to an e-value using a p-to-e calibrator and then back to p-value using an e-to-p calibrator generally loses quite a lot of evidence. For instance, starting with p = 0.01 p=0.01 , a conversion with the p-to-e calibrator p ↦ p − 1 / 2 − 1 p\mapsto p^{-1/2}-1 gives e = 9 e=9 , and another conversion with the e-to-p calibrator e ↦ min ⁡ ( 1 / e , 1 ) e\mapsto\min(1/e,1) yields p ′ = 1 / 9 p^{\prime}=1/9 . Therefore, it is not recommended in practice to calibrate iteratively in both directions. A possible interpretation of the above results on calibrators is that e-variables and p-variables are connected via a very rough relation 1 / e ∼ p 1/e\sim p . In one direction, the statement is precise: the reciprocal (truncated to 1 if needed) of an e-variable is a p-variable by Proposition 2.4 . On the other hand, using a calibrator f ⁡ ( p ) = κ ​ p κ − 1 f(p)=\kappa p^{\kappa-1} in ( 2.1 ) with a small κ > 0 \kappa>0 and ignoring positive constant factors, we can see that the reciprocal of a p-variable is approximately an e-variable; this is also the case of ( 2.2 ). In fact, f ⁡ ( p ) ≤ 1 / p f(p)\leq 1/p for all p p when f f is a calibrator; otherwise ∫ 0 1 f ⁡ ( q ) ​ 𝑑 q ≥ p ​ f ​ ( p ) > 1 \int_{0}^{1}f(q)\mathrm{d}q\geq pf(p)>1 , conflicting the condition in Proposition 2.5 . However, f ⁡ ( p ) = 1 / p f(p)=1/p for a fixed p p is only possible in the extreme case f : q ↦ 𝟙 { q ∈ [ 0 , p ] } / p f:q\mapsto\mathds{1}_{\{q\in[0,p]\}}/p . In the rest of the book, we omit “p-to-e” when mentioning calibrators, unless we want to stress the direction. Although all calibrators in ( 2.1 )–( 2.5 ) are admissible, some are more useful. In hypothesis testing, very small p-values and very large e-values are interesting. Calibrators in ( 2.3 ), ( 2.4 ) and ( 2.5 ) penalize very small p-values more than ( 2.2 ), which can be seen from their asymptotic behaviour as p ↓ 0 p\downarrow 0 , and therefore they are less likely to produce very large e-values; the calibrator in ( 2.3 ) is even bounded by 2 2 for p ≠ 0 p\neq 0 . Nevertheless, they may be useful when we take the product of many independent e-values. We end this section with a simple property of admissible calibrators. It also explains why we choose the domain of the calibrators as [ 0 , ∞ ) [0,\infty) instead of [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , although its value is set to 0 0 for input p-values larger than 1 1 . This result will be useful for later results in Chapter 12 . The next result states that any e-variable E E for an atomless probability measure ℙ \mathbb{P} can be seen as some calibrator applied to an exact p-variable. Indeed, as we see from the proof of the result below, this calibrator is a transform of the quantile function of E E .

mechanisms.text: A randomized test is a test that utilizes independent external randomization. It is possible to improve Markov’s inequality using external randomization, and this has direct implications for converting e-variables into tests or p-variables. The proof is simple. Since U U is uniform and independent of Y Y , we get yielding the claim. The first equality in ( 2.6 ) becomes an inequality ≤ \leq if U U is stochastically larger than standard uniform, and in particular U = 1 U=1 yields an alternative proof of Markov’s inequality. Also, if Y Y is bounded, that is Y ∈ [ 0 , C ] Y\in[0,C] almost surely for some C > 0 C>0 , then the inequality in ( 2.6 ) holds with equality for any α ≤ 1 / C \alpha\leq 1/C . In contrast, Markov’s inequality holds with equality only for distributions supported on { 0 , 1 / α } \{0,1/\alpha\} . The following corollary is a direct consequence of Theorem 2.9 , which offers additional interpretations of the relation between p-variables, e-variables, and randomization. Since U < 1 U<1 almost surely, U / E U/E is a strictly smaller p-value than 1 / E 1/E in all but degenerate cases. Thus, the corresponding randomized test is typically strictly more powerful than the non-randomized one. Said differently, e ↦ ( U / e ) ∧ 1 e\mapsto(U/e)\wedge 1 can be seen as a randomized e-to-p calibrator . In fact, this randomized e-to-p calibrator is admissible (treated in Section 11.3 ) and it dominates e ↦ ( 1 / e ) ∧ 1 e\mapsto(1/e)\wedge 1 , the latter only being admissible among non-randomized e-to-p calibrators (Proposition 2.4 ). A more general treatment of combining a p-value and an e-value is presented in Section 11.3 .

mechanisms.title: Admissible e-variables for a simple null are likelihood ratios / Characterization of admissibility
mechanisms.text: We first make a straightforward but important observation: For simple nulls, every admissible e-variable can be written as a likelihood ratio. We now characterize admissible e-variables for general 𝒫 \mathcal{P} . For A ∈ ℱ A\in\mathcal{F} and δ > 0 \delta>0 , let 𝒫 A δ = { ℙ ∈ 𝒫 : ℙ ⁡ ( A ) > δ } \mathcal{P}^{\delta}_{A}=\{\mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P}:\mathbb{P}(A)>\delta\} and 𝒫 A = { ℙ ∈ 𝒫 : ℙ ⁡ ( A ) > 0 } \mathcal{P}_{A}=\{\mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P}:\mathbb{P}(A)>0\} . The first result gives a simple necessary condition for admissible e-variables, which boils down to the exactness condition in Proposition 2.12 when 𝒫 = { ℙ } . \mathcal{P}=\{\mathbb{P}\}. Then next result gives a full characterization of admissible e-variables using its expectations under ℙ ∈ 𝒫 A δ \mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P}_{A}^{\delta} for A ∈ ℱ A\in\mathcal{F} . In this result, we use the convention inf ∅ = 0 \inf\varnothing=0 . Several sufficient conditions for ( 2.8 ) are easier to check, summarized in the next corollary. The condition (a) in Corollary 2.15 deserves some further attention. We will say that an e-variable is strongly admissible if condition (a) in Corollary 2.15 holds; note that (a) is implied by either of (b) and (c). mechanisms.text: Next, we consider e-variables defined on product spaces. Let 𝒫 ′ \mathcal{P}^{\prime} be a set of probabilities on another measurable space ( Ω ′ , ℱ ′ ) (\Omega^{\prime},\mathcal{F}^{\prime}) . We write 𝒫 × 𝒫 ′ \mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{P}^{\prime} for the set { ℙ × ℙ ′ : ℙ ∈ 𝒫 , ℙ ′ ∈ 𝒫 ′ } \{\mathbb{P}\times\mathbb{P}^{\prime}:\mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P},~\mathbb{P}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}^{\prime}\} of product probabilities. For E E on Ω \Omega and E ′ E^{\prime} on Ω ′ \Omega^{\prime} , let E × E ′ E\times E^{\prime} be defined by ( ω , ω ′ ) ↦ E ⁡ ( ω ) ​ E ′ ​ ( ω ′ ) (\omega,\omega^{\prime})\mapsto E(\omega)E^{\prime}(\omega^{\prime}) . Clearly, if E E is an e-variable for 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and E ′ E^{\prime} is an e-variable for 𝒫 ′ \mathcal{P}^{\prime} , then E × E ′ E\times E^{\prime} is an e-variable for 𝒫 × 𝒫 ′ \mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{P}^{\prime} , because for all ℙ ∈ 𝒫 \mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P} and ℙ ′ ∈ 𝒫 ′ \mathbb{P}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}^{\prime} . The next result further shows that E × E ′ E\times E^{\prime} is strongly admissible when E E and E ′ E^{\prime} are strongly admissible. Combining Propositions 2.16 and 2.17 , we obtain that E × E ′ E\times E^{\prime} is an admissible e-variable for admissible e-variables E E and E ′ E^{\prime} when 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and 𝒫 ′ \mathcal{P}^{\prime} are finite.

mechanisms.title: More examples of e-values
mechanisms.text: Continuing from the examples in Chapter 1 , we now provide several simple examples of e-values for different testing problems. Some of these e-values also enjoy a notion of optimality, introduced in Chapter 3 and analyzed in detail in Chapter 6 , so these examples will be revisited later in the book. In most examples below, we consider a single random observation (statistic) Z Z in a measurable space 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} and the sample space is chosen as ( Ω , ℱ ) = ( 𝒵 , σ ⁡ ( Z ) ) (\Omega,\mathcal{F})=(\mathcal{Z},\sigma(Z)) ; thus ℳ 1 \mathcal{M}_{1} is the set of all probability measures on σ ⁡ ( Z ) \sigma(Z) .

The same conclusion in Proposition 2.18 holds true for testing 𝒫 = { ℙ θ : θ ≥ θ 0 } \mathcal{P}=\{\mathbb{P}_{\theta}:\theta\geq\theta_{0}\} against 𝒬 = { ℙ θ : θ ≤ θ 1 } \mathcal{Q}=\{\mathbb{P}_{\theta}:\theta\leq\theta_{1}\} with θ 0 > θ 1 \theta_{0}>\theta_{1} ; moreover, either inequality (or both) in 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} can be replaced by a strict inequality. The same e-variable can also be used to test 𝒫 = { ℙ θ : θ ≤ θ 0 } \mathcal{P}=\{\mathbb{P}_{\theta}:\theta\leq\theta_{0}\} against 𝒬 = { ℙ θ : θ > θ 0 } . \mathcal{Q}=\{\mathbb{P}_{\theta}:\theta>\theta_{0}\}. The example of normal distributions in Section 1.6 satisfies the monotone likelihood ratio assumption. Therefore, the e-variable in ( 1.2 ) for any μ > 0 \mu>0 is an e-variable for testing { N ⁡ ( θ , 1 ) : θ ≤ 0 } \{\mathrm{N}(\theta,1):\theta\leq 0\} against { N ⁡ ( θ , 1 ) : θ > 0 } \{\mathrm{N}(\theta,1):\theta>0\} . An important special case is given by one-parameter exponential families, which we discuss further in Section 6.7.1 . There, and in Section 6.7.2 , we will argue that the above e-variable is actually log-optimal for ℚ = ℙ θ 1 \mathbb{Q}=\mathbb{P}_{\theta_{1}} for any θ 1 > θ 0 \theta_{1}>\theta_{0} , simply because p θ 1 / p θ 0 p_{\theta_{1}}/p_{\theta_{0}} is an e-variable for 𝒫 \mathcal{P} .

mechanisms.title: Testing sub-Gaussian means
mechanisms.text: Now take 𝒵 = ℝ \mathcal{Z}=\mathbb{R} and consider the null hypothesis that the observation Z Z has a 1-sub-Gaussian distribution with nonpositive mean. This class is a nonparametric generalization of Gaussians with nonpositive mean and unit variance. Formally, we set Here the sub-Gaussian restriction is only placed on the right tail. For ℙ ∈ 𝒫 \mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P} and λ ∈ ℝ \lambda\in\mathbb{R} , let M ℙ ​ ( λ ) = 𝔼 ℙ ​ [ e λ ​ Z ] M_{\mathbb{P}}(\lambda)=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[e^{\lambda Z}] , which is the moment generating function of Z Z . The constraint in 𝒫 \mathcal{P} means A Taylor expansion in a neighborhood of λ = 0 \lambda=0 yields, Therefore, for λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 small enough, and this implies 𝔼 ℙ ​ [ Z ] ≤ 0 \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[Z]\leq 0 . Since the standard Gaussian distribution (zero mean, unit variance) satisfy the above with equality (inferred via their moment generating function) for every real λ \lambda , the constraint expands the class to account for two aspects: the mean can be negative, and the right tails of the random variable only have to be lighter than that of a unit-variance Gaussian. It is well-known that any bounded distribution on [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] with zero mean is 1-sub-Gaussian; so the class 𝒫 \mathcal{P} clearly does not have any common reference measure, containing discrete distributions with uncountable support as well as continuous unbounded distributions. A class of e-variables for 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is given by: and certainly any convex combinations (mixtures) of its elements are also e-variables. The determination of the optimal e-variable against a specific ℚ \mathbb{Q} is studied in Section 6.7.5 . The determination of all possible e-variables for 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is a nontrivial task. We also consider the closely related null hypothesis that the observation Z Z has a 1-sub-Gaussian distribution with zero (instead of nonpositive) mean: Here, the sub-Gaussian restriction is placed on both the left and the right tails. Every ℙ ∈ 𝒫 0 \mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P}^{0} has zero mean, because now ( 2.13 ) holds for both positive and negative λ \lambda . Again, a natural class of e-variables for 𝒫 0 \mathcal{P}^{0} is and certainly any convex combinations (mixtures) of its elements are also e-variables. It turns out that every ℙ ∈ 𝒫 0 \mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P}^{0} also has variance bounded by one, and this follows from ( 2.13 ) with 𝔼 ℙ ​ [ Z ] = 0 \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[Z]=0 . Thus, Z 2 Z^{2} is also an e-variable, as is any convex combination with the aforementioned class. Indeed, 𝒫 0 \mathcal{P}^{0} is a subset of the hypothesis in ( 2.12 ) with μ = 0 \mu=0 and σ = 1 \sigma=1 , and also a subset of the one-sided sub-Gaussian class 𝒫 \mathcal{P} . However, Z 2 Z^{2} is not an e-variable for 𝒫 \mathcal{P} , because those could potentially have very heavy left tails, meaning that their variance is not necessarily bounded. We note in passing that both the above classes of e-variables are admissible, but the rather technical proof is omitted.

mechanisms.text: Many of the above examples of 𝒫 \mathcal{P} , and many others we encounter in this book, can be called “constrained hypotheses”, meaning that they are defined via integral constraints. For such classes, we can sometimes cleanly characterize the set of all e-variables (and all admissible ones) in terms of those constraints. Let ℒ \mathcal{L} denote the set of all real-valued measurable functions on the underlying probability space. A constraint set is any nonempty set of functions Ψ ⊆ ℒ \Psi\subseteq\mathcal{L} . We start with the case where Ψ = { g 1 , … , g K } \Psi=\{g_{1},\dots,g_{K}\} is finite, as in the case of testing a mean, or mean and variance. One can show that the set of all e-variables 𝔈 \mathfrak{E} for 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is given by all [ 0 , ∞ ] [0,\infty] -valued measurable functions which are 𝒫 \mathcal{P} -quasi surely dominated by 1 + ∑ k = 1 K π k ​ g k 1+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_{k}g_{k} for some π ∈ ℝ + K \pi\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{K} . As a corollary, every admissible e-variable for 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is 𝒫 \mathcal{P} -quasi surely equal to 1 + ∑ k = 1 K π k ​ g k 1+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_{k}g_{k} for some π \pi in the set Clearly, the zero vector 𝟎 \mathbf{0} is in Π Ψ \Pi^{\Psi} . But for some choices of Ψ \Psi , Π Ψ \Pi^{\Psi} may be equal to { 𝟎 } \{\mathbf{0}\} , in which case all e-variables for 𝒫 \mathcal{P} are dominated by the constant 1 1 . In settings where Ψ \Psi is infinite, such as the sub-Gaussian example in the previous subsection, the corresponding statement is more complex. Define where cone ​ ( Ψ ) \text{cone}(\Psi) is the conic hull of Ψ \Psi . Then, the set of all e-variables 𝔈 \mathfrak{E} for 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is given by all [ 0 , ∞ ] [0,\infty] -valued measurable functions that are 𝒫 \mathcal{P} -quasi surely equal to 1 + f 1+f for some f ∈ 𝒞 ¯ f\in\overline{\mathcal{C}} , where 𝒞 ¯ \overline{\mathcal{C}} is the weak closure of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} (which is the closure with respect to a particular weak topology that is omitted here for brevity). The constraints in ( 2.14 ) are formulated via integrals of f ∈ Ψ f\in\Psi over ℙ \mathbb{P} . In some applications, the constraints are formulated via other functionals, such as risk measures, and some of them are studied in Chapter 16 .

mechanisms.text: Let 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} be a general sample space. To interpret, testing 𝒫 \mathcal{P} means to test whether the true data-generating distribution is close to a given benchmark distribution ℙ 0 \mathbb{P}_{0} in terms of likelihood ratio being bounded by γ \gamma . The case γ = 1 \gamma=1 corresponds to the simple null hypothesis { ℙ 0 } \{\mathbb{P}_{0}\} . mechanisms.title: Testing exchangeability
mechanisms.text: Let 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} be arbitrary, and suppose Z = ( Z 1 , … , Z n ) Z=(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{n}) . Denote by 𝒮 n \mathcal{S}_{n} the set of all permutations of the set [ n ] [n] . For any σ ∈ 𝒮 n \sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{n} , let Z σ Z_{\sigma} denote the permuted vector ( Z σ ⁡ ( 1 ) , … , Z σ ⁡ ( n ) ) (Z_{\sigma(1)},\dots,Z_{\sigma(n)}) . mechanisms.title: Informal grids for realized e-values
mechanisms.text: In testing scientific hypotheses, thresholds for p-values are often chosen as 0.01 0.01 or 0.05 0.05 which correspond to type-I errors controlled at these levels. The e-to-p calibrator e ↦ min ⁡ ( 1 / e , 1 ) e\mapsto\min(1/e,1) implies that thresholds of 100 100 and 20 20 for e-values also have the above type-I error control. However, it is not recommended in practice to directly use these thresholds as the conversion e ↦ min ⁡ ( 1 / e , 1 ) e\mapsto\min(1/e,1) is typically wasteful. In Section 1.5 , and also in Section 4.1 later, we see that for a ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) a\in(0,1) , an e-value of 1 / a 1/a carries more information than a p-value of a a . In order to judge how significant results of testing using e-values are, the type-I error, based on which p-values are defined, may not be the desirable metric. Although there are no universally agreed thresholds to use for e-values, the rule of thumb of Jeffreys, originally designed for likelihood ratios, may offer some insight, as e-values are generalizations of likelihood ratios (for example, recall the result presented in Section 2.5.1 ). We summarize this rule of thumb in Table 2.19 . For instance, if e > 3.16 e>3.16 , we recommend to associate it with “substantial” (similar to p < 0.05 p<0.05 ), and if e > 10 e>10 , we recommend to associate it with “strong” (similar to p < 0.01 p<0.01 ). One should keep in mind that p-values and e-values do not have a one-to-one correspondence with each other, and the interpretation of the informal grid for e-values does not rely on converting into p-values. Because Jeffreys focused on likelihood ratios (or Bayes factors), the above rule of thumb applies well to e-values that are obtained “naturally”, such as likelihood ratios or their generalizations in the subsequent chapters. At the other extreme, for all-or-nothing e-variables (see Definition 3.5 ), such as E = 𝟙 { P ≤ α } / α E=\mathds{1}_{\{P\leq\alpha\}}/\alpha for some p-variable P P , one should not refer to the grids in Table 2.19 , because for such an e-variable, E = 10 E=10 is equivalent to P ≤ 0.1 P\leq 0.1 . Finally, Section 6.6 draws deeper connections between e-values and Bayes factors, but it builds on some more advanced material. It is important to note that in general, p-values and e-values need not even “point in the same direction”. We can easily have situations where the p-value appears to provide strong evidence against the null, but the e-value supports the null, or vice versa. Let us elaborate with a simple example. Consider testing μ = 0 \mu=0 against μ = δ \mu=\delta (for some δ > 0 \delta>0 ) when we see data Z ∼ N ⁡ ( μ , 1 ) Z\sim N(\mu,1) . Since the classic z z -test is uniformly most powerful in this setting, we would get the same p-value P = 1 − Φ ⁡ ( Z ) P=1-\Phi(Z) , regardless of the alternative mean δ \delta , while the (arguably natural) likelihood ratio e-value E = exp ⁡ ( δ ​ Z − δ 2 / 2 ) E=\exp(\delta Z-\delta^{2}/2) depends strongly on δ \delta . For instance, with δ = 5 \delta=5 and X = 2 X=2 , the p-value P ≈ 0.023 P\approx 0.023 (suggesting evidence against the null), but the e-value E ≈ 0.08 E\approx 0.08 (suggesting evidence for the null as a likelihood ratio). Thus the realized p-value and e-value could “point in different directions” depending on δ \delta and the realized data. This is another reason that we do not like to in general compare e-value and p-value based methods: while calibration can often preserve the direction (large/small e-values yield small/large p-values and vice versa), natural p-values and e-values that we may directly construct from the data need not have any natural concordance with each other, and so the resulting methods are not always directly comparable.

mechanisms.title: Bibliographical note
mechanisms.text: This chapter largely resembles results and concepts in various important papers on e-values, but also it contains many results that are derived for the book to make a coherent piece. The example in Section 2.1 is based on Vovk and Wang (2023) . The concept of a calibrator in Section 2.3 dates back, at least, to Vovk (1993) ; the admissibility results are in Vovk and Wang (2021) . Bickel (2025) discussed p-to-e calibrators that depend on the sample size based on Bayes factors. Section 2.4 is based on Ignatiadis et al. (2024b) and Ramdas and Manole (2025) . The definition of admissibility in Section 2.5 is derived from Ramdas et al. (2020) , which studies it more generally in sequential settings. Some sufficient conditions in Corollary 2.15 also follow from the aforementioned paper. Among the examples in Section 2.6 , exponential families and monotone likelihood ratios were studied by Grünwald et al. (2024a) ; Grünwald et al. (2024b) . The testing symmetry example was first studied by Ramdas et al. (2020) , with follow-up work in Koning (2023b) ; Vovk and Wang (2024b) ; Larsson et al. (2025a) . The bounded mean example is a variant of one studied in Waudby-Smith and Ramdas (2024) , revisited by Larsson et al. (2025a) . The mean-and-variance example was studied by Fan et al. (2025) . Sub-Gaussian e-values were studied by Howard et al. (2020) ; Ramdas et al. (2020) ; Larsson et al. (2025a) . The example on constrained hypotheses was studied by Clerico (2024) ; Larsson et al. (2025b) ; our presentation is based on the latter. The exchangeability example was studied in Vovk (2021) and Ramdas et al. (2022) in a sequential context. In the batch context, the soft-rank e-value was proposed in the first arXiv preprint of Wang and Ramdas (2022) (but omitted in the journal version), and revisited by Koning (2023b) . The grids in Section 2.7 can be found in ( Jeffreys, 1961 , Appendix B) , with a variant proposed in Kass and Raftery (1995) .

mechanisms.locator: §Chapter 3 Efficiency: E-values under the alternative hypothesis
mechanisms.title: Efficiency: E-values under the alternative hypothesis
mechanisms.text:
In Chapter 2 we focused only on the properties of the e-values under the null hypothesis. In this chapter, we describe its desired properties under the alternative hypothesis. This requires the notions of powered e-values, e-power, and log-optimality. The power of a test ϕ \phi against an alternative ℚ \mathbb{Q} is simply 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ ϕ ] \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\phi] . The type-II error (rate) of ϕ \phi equals one minus its power. When testing a null hypothesis 𝒫 \mathcal{P} , a test ϕ \phi is powered at level α ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \alpha\in(0,1) against 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} if and it is uniformly powered if further inf ℚ ∈ 𝒬 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ ϕ ] > α \inf_{\mathbb{Q}\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\phi]>\alpha . mechanisms.title: Powered tests, e-values, and p-values
mechanisms.text: We first introduce the concept of power for tests and e-values. The power of a binary test ϕ \phi against ℚ \mathbb{Q} is defined as the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis under the alternative ℚ \mathbb{Q} . This concept can be naturally generalized to non-binary tests as we present below. When we mention a powered test ϕ \phi without specifying the level, it should be understood as α = sup ℙ ∈ 𝒫 𝔼 ℙ ​ [ ϕ ] \alpha=\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[\phi] . Tests that are not powered can still be practically useful. For instance, the existence of powered tests and e-variables requires that the alternative 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} does not contain a “boundary point” of the null 𝒫 \mathcal{P} , as shown by Example 3.3 below. Nevertheless, although powered tests do not exist for testing H 0 : μ < 0 H_{0}:\mu<0 against H 1 : μ ≥ 0 H_{1}:\mu\geq 0 in that example, any powered test for testing H 0 H_{0} against H 1 ′ : μ > 0 H^{\prime}_{1}:\mu>0 can still be useful to test H 0 H_{0} against H 1 H_{1} in practical applications. Next, we discuss the natural connection between e-values and tests. Given any level- α \alpha binary test, one can always reproduce its decision by combining an “all-or-nothing e-value” with Markov’s inequality, as we explain (and generalize) below. All-or-nothing e-variables take on only two values: zero or 1 / c 1/c for some c c . Further, it is clear that A A must satisfy ℙ ⁡ ( A ) ≤ c \mathbb{P}(A)\leq c for all ℙ ∈ 𝒫 \mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P} . For such e-variables, Markov’s inequality at level c c holds with equality, so there is no loss in translating between e-values, tests, and p-values. As a consequence of Fact 3.6 , all binary tests based on p-values — routinely used in the sciences — can be replicated using e-values. A non-binary test ϕ \phi is usually provided with the interpretation that it outputs a rejection with probability ϕ \phi , realized as a number in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . In other words, one can convert a non-binary test ϕ \phi to a binary test ϕ ′ \phi^{\prime} as ϕ ′ = 𝟙 { U ≤ ϕ } \phi^{\prime}=\mathds{1}_{\{U\leq\phi\}} , where U U is an independent uniform random variable on [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . This is closely related to the randomized Markov’s inequality discussed in Section 2.4 . An e-variable E E taking values in [ 0 , 1 / α ] [0,1/\alpha] is associated with a level- α \alpha test ϕ = α ​ E \phi=\alpha E ; in fact, it also yields a level- β \beta test for any β < α \beta<\alpha . A single e-variable yields a family of level- α \alpha tests (indexed by α \alpha ), but in the other direction, every level- α \alpha test yields a different e-variable. The above discussion highlights an important conceptual point — e-values suffice for testing: If a problem is testable (i.e., a powered test exists), then it is testable with e-values. This also applies to a notion of powered p-variables, although it is conceptually slightly more complicated, as we define below. For practical purposes, it is more than sufficient to consider β = 0.25 \beta=0.25 , for example, as rejections via p-values are always done at small levels. In the next section, we will connect powered tests, powered e-variables, and powered p-variables.

mechanisms.title: E-power and powered e-values
mechanisms.text: Given this high-level equivalence between tests and bounded e-values discussed in Fact 3.6 , one may be tempted to ask: What is new here? Are we just simply working with tests in disguise? The answer is this: While all-or-nothing e-values are interesting conceptually in order to relate them to tests and p-values, these are not typically how one would construct e-values in practice. Recall the example from Section 1.6 on likelihood ratios. They will commonly have support on the entire positive real line (not just on two points), and never take on the value zero if ℙ \mathbb{P} and ℚ \mathbb{Q} are absolutely continuous with respect to each other. To explain this, the following concept of e-power is useful. The e-power of an e-variable could equal ∞ \infty or − ∞ -\infty (these still count as being well-defined). Indeed, whenever we make statements involving expected logarithms, we require them to be well-defined. The e-power (higher is better) of all-or-nothing e-variables is − ∞ -\infty . The concept of e-power is closely related to the Kelly criterion in betting and investment. The logarithm reflects the fact that in many applications, e-values are multiplied together. For a simplest example, consider a sequence of iid e-variables E 1 , E 2 , … E_{1},E_{2},\dots with finite e-power and the process M = ( M t ) t ∈ ℕ M=(M_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}} defined by The e-power of E 1 E_{1} against ℚ \mathbb{Q} equals the asymptotic growth rate of M M , that is, the ℚ \mathbb{Q} -almost sure limit of ( log ⁡ M t ) / t (\log M_{t})/t as t → ∞ t\to\infty (see Definition 7.4 ), justified by the strong law of large numbers. The asymptotic growth rate will be important in the methodology of testing by betting, formally treated in Chapter 7 . When converting M t M_{t} into the level- α \alpha test 𝟙 { M t ≥ 1 / α } \mathds{1}_{\{M_{t}\geq 1/\alpha\}} for α ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \alpha\in(0,1) , the role of e-power is clear from the following proposition. The proof of Proposition 3.12 is a simple application of the strong law of large numbers. Note that for each t ∈ ℕ t\in\mathbb{N} , E 1 E_{1} has positive e-power against ℚ \mathbb{Q} is and only if M t M_{t} has positive e-power against ℚ \mathbb{Q} . Proposition 3.12 implies that in the simple iid setting, a positive e-power leads to asymptotic power- 1 1 tests, and a negative e-power leads to asymptotic power- 0 0 tests. An axiomatic justification of e-power is presented in Section 3.8 , which uses an axiom based on an idea that is similar to Proposition 3.12 . The condition 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ log ⁡ E ] > 0 \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log E]>0 in Definition 3.11 is equivalent to saying that the geometric mean of X X is larger than one: exp ⁡ 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ log ⁡ E ] > 1 \exp\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log E]>1 , which is a stronger constraint than requiring the (arithmetic) mean of E E to be larger than 1, that is, 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ E ] > 1 \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[E]>1 in Definition 3.1 (this can be seen from Jensen’s inequality). Hence, if E E has positive e-power, then E E is a powered e-variable, but the reverse implication is not true in general. These two conditions are closely related. mechanisms.title: Conditions for the existence of powered e-variables
mechanisms.text: In this section, we address the existence of powered e-variables and p-variables by means of two characterization results. These results connect the existence of p-variables and e-variables to the structure of the null and alternative hypotheses, different from Theorem 3.9 , which does not discuss how to check the existence. In these results, let L L and M M be two positive integers and we continue to assume ( U ) in Section 3.2 . The following result uses the total variation distance between sets of distributions, which we now define. For any two distributions ℙ , ℚ \mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q} , define where the supremum is taken over all measurable sets A A . Then, given two sets of distributions 𝒫 , 𝒬 \mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q} , we can define The following result is closely connected to a classic theorem of Kraft (1955) , proved by Le Cam in private communication. The Kraft–Le Cam theorem states that for general 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} (not necessarily finite) that have a common reference measure, the following holds: for any ε ≥ 0 \varepsilon\geq 0 , there exists a test ϕ \phi such that inf ℚ ∈ 𝒬 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ ϕ ] − sup ℙ ∈ 𝒫 𝔼 ℙ ​ [ ϕ ] > ε \inf_{\mathbb{Q}\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\phi]-\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[\phi]>\varepsilon if and only if the total variation distance between the closed convex hulls of 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} is greater than 2 ​ ε 2\varepsilon . there exists a test ϕ \phi such that inf ℚ ∈ 𝒬 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ ϕ ] > sup ℙ ∈ 𝒫 𝔼 ℙ ​ [ ϕ ] \inf_{\mathbb{Q}\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\phi]>\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[\phi] ; there exists a uniformly powered bounded e-variable E E for 𝒫 \mathcal{P} against 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} ; d TV ​ ( Conv ⁡ ( 𝒫 ) , Conv ⁡ ( 𝒬 ) ) > 0 d_{\text{TV}}(\mathrm{Conv}(\mathcal{P}),\mathrm{Conv}(\mathcal{Q}))>0 . If there is no common reference measure, then condition (iii) is not equivalent to the earlier ones. In fact, even when 𝒬 = { ℚ } \mathcal{Q}=\{\mathbb{Q}\} is simple, d TV ​ ( Conv ⁡ ( 𝒫 ) , ℚ ) > 0 d_{\text{TV}}(\mathrm{Conv}(\mathcal{P}),\mathbb{Q})>0 does not imply the existence of a powered e-variable. The appropriate condition actually involves an object called the bipolar of 𝒫 \mathcal{P} , and is formally presented in Theorem 6.10 . Separately, note that when 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} are finite, condition (iii) above reduces to Conv ⁡ ( ℚ 1 , … , ℚ M ) ∩ Conv ⁡ ( ℙ 1 , … , ℙ L ) = ∅ \mathrm{Conv}(\mathbb{Q}_{1},\dots,\mathbb{Q}_{M})\cap\mathrm{Conv}(\mathbb{P}_{1},\dots,\mathbb{P}_{L})=\varnothing . The existence of exact p-variables and e-variables is technically more advanced, and studied in Section 14.3 , where we obtain a similar result (Theorem 14.6 ) to Theorem 3.17 .

mechanisms.title: Log-optimality and likelihood ratios
mechanisms.text: Next, we turn to the key concept of log-optimality for a simple alternative { ℚ } \{\mathbb{Q}\} , which is defined essentially via the comparison of e-power. Definitions 3.11 and 3.18 are obviously connected. If the maximum e-power, defined as is finite, then the log-optimal e-variable maximizes the e-power, and the definition of log-optimality reduces to saying 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ log ⁡ E ′ ] ≤ 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ log ⁡ E ] \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log E^{\prime}]\leq\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log E] . The current definition allows the maximum e-power to be infinite, which could occur even in simple cases such as testing a Gaussian against a Cauchy because the tails of the Cauchy are much heavier than that of the Gaussian; see also Example 3.16 . Note that 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ log ⁡ ( E ′ / E ) ] ≤ 0 \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log(E^{\prime}/E)]\leq 0 and 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ log ⁡ ( E ′ ) ] ≤ 𝔼 ℚ ​ [ log ⁡ ( E ) ] \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log(E^{\prime})]\leq\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log(E)] are equivalent when E E and E ′ E^{\prime} have finite e-power, but the two conditions are not equivalent in general. We do not prove the first part in this book, since the proof is quite technical, and defer the second part to Chapter 6 . However, in the case of a simple null hypothesis ℙ \mathbb{P} with ℚ ≪ ℙ \mathbb{Q}\ll\mathbb{P} , existence and uniqueness of the log-optimal e-variable can be easily argued, as we will see in Theorem 3.20 . In this section, we present an important result on the log-optimal e-values for a simple null hypothesis 𝒫 = { ℙ } \mathcal{P}=\{\mathbb{P}\} and a simple alternative 𝒬 = { ℚ } \mathcal{Q}=\{\mathbb{Q}\} . We will assume that ℚ ≪ ℙ \mathbb{Q}\ll\mathbb{P} . Let q q and p p represent the densities of ℚ \mathbb{Q} and ℙ \mathbb{P} with respect to some reference measure 𝕃 \mathbb{L} , by which we can write ( d ​ ℚ / d ​ ℙ ) ​ ( x ) = q ⁡ ( x ) / p ⁡ ( x ) ({\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}}/{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}})(x)={q(x)}/{p(x)} . The classic Neyman–Pearson lemma for hypothesis testing states that when testing a simple null ℙ \mathbb{P} against a simple alternative ℚ \mathbb{Q} , the most powerful level- α \alpha test involves thresholding the likelihood ratio. We now present a result that can be seen as the e-analog of the Neyman–Pearson lemma. Importantly, we are not interested in designing tests (which can be obtained via Markov’s inequality as discussed in Chapter 2 ), but simply in designing e-variable that is log-optimal (as e-powerful as possible). To prepare for the statement, define the Kullback–Leibler divergence between ℚ \mathbb{Q} and ℙ \mathbb{P} as where it is defined as ∞ \infty if ℚ \mathbb{Q} is not absolutely continuous with respect to ℙ \mathbb{P} . Gibbs’ inequality, or the Shannon–Kolmogorov information inequality, states that the Kullback–Leibler divergence between any two distributions is nonnegative: KL ⁡ ( ℚ , ℙ ) ≥ 0 \mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{P})\geq 0 . Further, equality holds if and only if ℙ = ℚ \mathbb{P}=\mathbb{Q} . In Chapter 6 , we present a more general result encompassing Theorem 3.20 , which even relaxes the assumption ℚ ≪ ℙ \mathbb{Q}\ll\mathbb{P} .
